title: Surveys and Sampling: How Data Is Collected Fairly

questions.question: The entire group of individuals a study is about is called the:
questions.rationale: The population is every unit of interest; the sample is only the subset actually studied.

questions.question: The list from which a sample is actually drawn is the:
questions.rationale: The sampling frame is the accessible list of units; when it omits part of the population, undercoverage bias results.

questions.question: To take a systematic sample of 25 students from a list of 200, the sampling interval k is:
questions.rationale: k = N/n = 200/25 = 8, so every 8th name after a random start between 1 and 8 is selected.

questions.question: A school has 800, 700, and 500 students in grades 9, 10, and 11. A proportional stratified sample of 100 gives grade 10:
questions.rationale: Each stratum contributes n × (stratum size / N) = 100 × 700/2000 = 35; grades 9 and 11 get 40 and 25.

questions.question: A researcher wants to guarantee that each of several known, contrasting subgroups appears in fair proportion. The best method is:
questions.rationale: Stratified sampling divides the population into non-overlapping strata and samples each in proportion to its size.

questions.question: A health team surveys households scattered across 50 villages by randomly choosing 5 villages and studying households inside them. This is:
questions.rationale: Whole natural groups (clusters) are selected at random and units are studied within them — cluster sampling.

questions.question: A number computed from a sample, such as the sample mean, is used to estimate the corresponding:
questions.rationale: A statistic estimates the population parameter; the gap between them is sampling error, which shrinks as the sample grows.

questions.question: The 1936 Literary Digest poll gathered 2.4 million ballots yet predicted the wrong US president, mainly because:
options: the sample was far too small
its voter list reached wealthier citizens far more often (selection bias)
questions.rationale: A huge but biased sample loses to an unbiased small one: the frame systematically under-represented lower-income voters.

questions.question: Asking "Do you agree the canteen should finally serve healthy food?" is an example of:
questions.rationale: The word "finally" pushes respondents towards agreement — the question's wording itself shapes the answer.

questions.question: Increasing the size of a properly drawn random sample will reduce:
questions.rationale: Bigger random samples reduce sampling error, but bias comes from how the sample was chosen and asked — size cannot fix it.
